title: Abstract inner-product setting
content: Works over an arbitrary real inner-product space F (NormedAddCommGroup + InnerProductSpace ℝ F), not just the Euclidean plane, and opens the parent EulerInequalityHeronOQ06 namespace to reuse its circumradius, inradius, area and semiperimeter definitions. The genuine geometry — points and Euclidean distances — lives in F, distinguishing this entry from the parent's pure side-length model.
mathContext: $F$ is any real inner-product space; $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{\mathbb R}$ denotes its real inner product and $\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$. The vertices $A,B,C$ and centres $O,I$ are honest points of $F$.

title: weighted_sum_norm_sq — the Gram-expansion core
content: For three vectors u, v, w of common norm R with pairwise distances a = ‖v−w‖, b = ‖w−u‖, c = ‖u−v‖, proves ‖a·u + b·v + c·w‖² = R²(a+b+c)² − abc(a+b+c). First extracts the three Gram inner products ⟪u,v⟫ = R²−c²/2, ⟪v,w⟫ = R²−a²/2, ⟪u,w⟫ = R²−b²/2 from the polarization identity norm_sub_sq_real, then expands ‖·‖² via real_inner_self_eq_norm_sq, normalizes orientations with real_inner_comm, and finishes with ring. This single identity is the entire geometric content of Euler's theorem.
mathContext: Polarization: $\|u-v\|^2=\|u\|^2-2\langle u,v\rangle+\|v\|^2$ gives $\langle u,v\rangle=R^2-\tfrac{c^2}{2}$ (and cyclically). Expanding $\|a u+b v+c w\|^2=\sum a^2\|u\|^2+2\sum ab\langle u,v\rangle$ and substituting, the cross terms $2ab\langle u,v\rangle+2bc\langle v,w\rangle+2ca\langle u,w\rangle$ collapse to $-abc(a+b+c)$, leaving $R^2(a+b+c)^2-abc(a+b+c)$.

title: incenter_dist_circumcenter_sq — the area-free Euler core
content: For a triangle ABC with circumcenter O at distance R from each vertex and incenter I = (a·A+b·B+c·C)/(a+b+c), proves OI² = R² − abc/(a+b+c). Passes to position vectors u = A−O, v = B−O, w = C−O (each of norm R via dist_eq_norm'), rewrites the side lengths as their norms, and crucially shows I − O = (a+b+c)⁻¹·(a·u+b·v+c·w) — valid because the barycentric weights sum to (a+b+c), handled by the module tactic. Then dist O I² = norm_smul · weighted_sum_norm_sq, finished by field_simp. No area, no square roots.
mathContext: Since the incenter weights sum to 1, $I-O=(a+b+c)^{-1}(a u+b v+c w)$, so $OI^2=\dfrac{\|a u+b v+c w\|^2}{(a+b+c)^2}=\dfrac{R^2(a+b+c)^2-abc(a+b+c)}{(a+b+c)^2}=R^2-\dfrac{abc}{a+b+c}$.

title: two_circumradius_mul_inradius — the algebraic bridge
content: Proves 2·R·r = abc/(a+b+c) in the side-length model, where R = circumradius a b c = abc/(4·Area) and r = inradius a b c = Area/s. Unfolds the definitions, uses area_pos (Heron's area is positive for a genuine triangle, from the triangle inequalities), and clears denominators with field_simp; the Area factors cancel and ring closes. This is the sole place the area enters — and it disappears.
mathContext: $2Rr=2\cdot\dfrac{abc}{4\,\mathrm{Area}}\cdot\dfrac{\mathrm{Area}}{s}=\dfrac{abc}{2s}=\dfrac{abc}{a+b+c}$, using $s=\tfrac{a+b+c}{2}$. The $\mathrm{Area}$ cancels exactly, so the bridge is a pure rational identity in $a,b,c$.

title: euler_OI_sq — Euler's triangle formula OI² = R² − 2Rr
content: The headline result: with O, I, A, B, C honest points and R the circumradius, OI² = R² − 2·R·r. The proof simply rewrites with the Euler core incenter_dist_circumcenter_sq to get OI² = R² − abc/(a+b+c), then substitutes the bridge two_circumradius_mul_inradius backwards (via hcirc : R = circumradius a b c) to convert abc/(a+b+c) into 2Rr. The geometric and algebraic halves meet here.
mathContext: $OI^2=R^2-\dfrac{abc}{a+b+c}=R^2-2Rr$ — Euler's 1765 identity $d^2=R(R-2r)$, now as an honest squared Euclidean distance in $F$.

title: euler_inequality_of_dist — R ≥ 2r as OI² ≥ 0
content: Recovers Euler's inequality 2r ≤ R geometrically. From euler_OI_sq, R² − 2Rr = OI² ≥ 0 (sq_nonneg). With R > 0 (positivity, since the circumradius abc/(4·Area) is positive for a genuine triangle), nlinarith concludes R ≥ 2r. The inequality is thus not an algebraic estimate but the literal nonnegativity of a squared distance — exactly Euler's intended meaning.
mathContext: $OI^2\ge 0$ and $OI^2=R^2-2Rr=R(R-2r)$, with $R>0$, force $R-2r\ge 0$, i.e. $R\ge 2r$, with equality iff $O=I$ (the equilateral case).
